power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Autistic masking has typically been understood as the suppression of natural Autistic traits within neuronormative social contexts.
However, social interactions are inherently embedded within broader sensory environments, highlighting the need to consider how sensory experiences shape masking processes.
Although sensory experiences have been recognized within existing masking research, the sensory dimensions of masking remain comparatively underexplored.

In this perspective, we examine sensory masking as an interrelated dimension of broader Autistic masking processes, defined as the conscious or subconscious suppression, inhibition, or override of sensory responses to meet environmental or social expectations.
Drawing on recent research and our own lived experience, we describe how these sensory dimensions may emerge developmentally, often as a learned adaptation to unsafe or invalidating experiences.
We then consider the cumulative effects of sustained sensory masking.

While sensory masking may serve a functional purpose, its chronic and persistent engagement may contribute to burnout and negatively impact well-being and mental health, particularly in the context of prolonged exposure to sensory aversive environments.

We also distinguish these sensory dimensions from related processes of sensory self-regulation and sensory unmasking, which involve supporting regulation and reclaiming autonomy through safe sensory self-expression.

We conclude by outlining constructive approaches that support sensory safety, self-regulation, and well-being, and propose future research directions to explore the mechanisms, impacts, and potential supports associated with the sensory dimensions of masking.

A utistic masking has most commonly been discussed within broader frameworks of camouflaging, which describe the conscious or subconscious use of strategies to minimize the visibility of autistic traits in social contexts. 1, 2 Within these frameworks, masking is often conceptualized alongside compensatory and assimilative strategies used to navigate neuronormative social expectations.

text.text: Nevertheless, social and communication experiencesand indeed, our very existence-are inherently sensory rich, shaped not only by social cues (e.g., gestures, voices, facial expressions) but also by the surrounding sensory environment (e.g., background noise, lighting) and our internal senses (e.g., interoceptive experiences such as body cues or feelings of overwhelm).

Given that sensory processing differences are a hallmark of Autistic neurocognition, 9 it is important to consider the totality of sensory experience and subsequent processing of information in the context of Autistic masking.

text.text: In this perspective, we explore the sensory dimensions of masking in autism, focusing on how sensory processing, regulation, and adaptation shape how masking is experienced.

While this perspective focuses on Autistic experience, we acknowledge that similar forms of sensory masking may also be present across other neurodivergent populations. 6 Drawing on research and the lived experiences of Autistic authors, we outline key features of these sensory processes and highlight directions for future research.

text.text: By explicitly considering the sensory dimensions of masking, we aim to broaden current conceptualizations of masking, highlight an underexplored aspect of Autistic experience, and identify priorities for future empirical research.

Social masking has received increasing attention in autism research over the past decade, describing how Autistic people often monitor and modify their behavior, language, and nonverbal cues to align with neuronormative expectations in everyday interactions. 2, 10, 11 However, ongoing debate remains regarding its conceptual boundaries, theoretical foundations, measurement, and relationship to related constructs such as impression management. [12] [13] [14] [15] [16] Recent integrative frameworks have further highlighted the multidimensional nature of masking and camouflaging, including not only behavioral strategies but differences in motivations, effort, ability, awareness, and the extent to which masking may become habitual or automatic. 17, 18 Despite this broader conceptualization, the sensory dimensions of masking remain comparatively underexplored.

text.text: Across these varied forms, masking can involve continuous self-regulation, imposing a heightened cognitive load on Autistic people. [19] [20] [21] [22] [23] Masking is typically examined in social contexts; however, social interaction is necessarily a sensory experience and shaped by the broader sensory environments in which it occurs. 21, 24, 25 These dimensions intersect in social contexts, where the sensory environment can be challenging and shape how interactions are experienced.

text.text: Masking may, therefore, involve the ongoing inhibition of sensory responses both within and beyond social contexts, alongside the regulation of behavior in social circumstances.

However, masking research has traditionally focused on social and communication characteristics, and has largely overlooked sensory experiences, which are also a core dimension of Autistic experience that may be masked.
Examples of this can be found within the existing masking literature.

Autistic people have described masking "sensory differences such as pain due to sounds," including one participant who described experiencing a weekly meltdown in response to the "extreme" noise and activity of a shopping center that was "carefully hidden as much as possible" 18 (p. 2384).

text.text: Separately, sensory environments may increase the cognitive and regulatory demands of masking, amplifying the effort required to navigate social situations.
Furthermore, sensory demands may interact with social demands, making masking more difficult to sustain in particular environments.
For example, in Miller et al., 4 a participant noted that "sensory processing difficulties, particularly auditory, make masking tougher" (p. 334).

text.text: Social interactions are almost never experienced in isolation from the sensory context: noise, lighting, or crowding, and the combined demands of social engagement and sensory masking can intensify cognitive fatigue and make participation far more effortful. [26] [27] [28] Like social masking, the persistent suppression or override of sensory responses can place substantial cognitive and emotional demands on Autistic people, with potential impacts on mental well-being, exhaustion, distress, and quality of life. 3, 29, 30

text.text: In this perspective, we focus on the sensory dimensions of masking, defined here as the conscious or subconscious suppression, inhibition, or override of sensory responses within everyday contexts.

For instance, to meet neuronormative expectations, Autistic people may suppress reflexive responses to sensory input, such as covering their ears, moving away from a distressing stimulus, or expressing discomfort, particularly when stimuli are experienced as overwhelming or unsafe (e.g., sudden noise or flickering lights).

In addition, this may include suppressing sensory responses that provide a selfregulatory function such as tapping, rocking, vocalizations, or reactions to stimuli that are perceived as aversive-especially in public or socially restrictive contexts. 5, 11, 31 We further propose that sensory masking may emerge, in part, through the repeated invalidation of Autistic sensory experiences from an early age.

text.text: This may occur through external feedback or through comparison with others, where one's own sensory responses are perceived as different or less valid. 32 Sensory masking not only involves the modulation of responses to external stimulus (e.g., sound, light, touch), but also the attenuation or reinterpretation of internal bodily signals (i.e., interoceptive signals), including states such as discomfort, overwhelm, or affective responses to sensory input. 30, 33, 34 Consequently, these responses may be enacted consciously or become increasingly automatic over time, evolving across the lifespan. 10, 35 Over time, this could involve reduced access to or trust in one's own interoceptive signals, as individuals learn to override internal cues in favor of externally expected responses. 33 The developmental shaping of sensory masking and adaptation.

text.text: Sensory masking is unlikely to emerge in early infancy or early toddlerhood, but rather appears to develop as a learned and conditioned response. 35 Young Autistic children are more likely to respond organically to overwhelming or aversive sensory stimuli.

text.text: Indeed, studies have consistently demonstrated a higher rate of observable sensory responses and distress, including meltdowns and shutdowns, in younger Autistic children compared with Autistic adults. [36] [37] [38] Drawing on the cascading developmental model, 35 we propose that, over time, Autistic young people may learn to suppress or mask their natural sensory responses due to repeated exposure to unpredictable sensory environments, direct or perceived invalidation of their instinctive responses, or emotional distress.

text.text: For example, a child who consistently experiences distress in response to loud auditory input may, over time, learn to inhibit visible reactions such as running away, ear covering, or vocalizing distress, often perceived as stigmatizing. 11 Similarly, children who seek or respond strongly to tactile (e.g., itchy uniform or clothing tag) or movement (e.g., chaotic classroom environment) input may gradually learn to hide or redirect these behaviors (even unknowingly) due to ongoing feedback from others, or from self-awareness that their response differs from others. [39] [40] [41] These patterns may initially be context-specific but can later become generalized across environments and modalities, particularly with repeated exposure. 42 Over time, as Autistic children navigate social expectations, environmental demands, or discouragement of their natural sensory responses, a gradual pattern of developmental suppression may begin to take root. 35, 43, 44 These adaptations can become internalized, resulting in automatic or subconscious suppression that can persist into adolescence and adulthood. 45 This perspective also aligns with concept of adaptive morphing, 3 which frames masking-related adaptations not as deliberate deception, but as biologically shaped and safety-driven responses that may emerge through lifelong conditioning.

text.text: For some Autistic people, sensory masking may develop as an adaptive response to previous experiences of punishment, bullying, invalidation, or exclusion following sensory expression.

For instance, an Autistic person may automatically ignore the discomfort of their work uniform as they have been repeatedly told that the rejection of school uniform is unacceptable. 39 Similarly, a loud, crowded room may not only overwhelm an Autistic person's sensory processing but also necessitate additional masking to navigate social interactions within that environment without drawing attention to their sensory distress.

text.text: Visible sensory responses should therefore not necessarily be interpreted as reflecting differences in social motivation or understanding, but may instead reflect the demands of navigating overwhelming sensory environments. 41, 54 As with social masking-which is often understood as a strategy for social survival and safety 2-5,10,55,56 -we suggest that sensory masking may similarly function as a survival mechanism.

text.text: It involves knowingly or unknowingly dismissing or suppressing instinctive sensory responses and replacing them with learned behaviors to maintain a sense of safety in one's environment.

These behaviors can reflect contextual demands, like wearing tactile-aversive clothing, 57 suppressing sensory overwhelm from noise or lighting to focus, 58 or navigating sensory challenges embedded within social interactions. 26 Just as social masking has been framed as a response to social risk, 4, 11 we argue that sensory masking similarly could reflect in-the-moment efforts to manage environmental threat and discomfort.

text.text: As people navigate through different life stages and face evolving environmental demands, the adaptive strategies employed to manage sensory experiences, including sensory masking, may undergo changes. 42, [59] [60] [61] This dynamic process involves adjustments in cognitive loading, as people develop new coping mechanisms or experience shifts in the effectiveness of existing strategies.

text.text: For some Autistic people, challenging sensory environments can contribute to overwhelm, distress, fatigue, and reduced capacity to engage, making the sensory context particularly relevant to understanding the demands of masking.
Like social masking, we acknowledge that sensory masking may often be necessary for Autistic people to feel safe and able to participate in community and social activities.
However, it can come at a cost.

When sensory input becomes overwhelming, sustained exposure may contribute to sensory overload, while the additional cognitive effort required to suppress or override sensory responses may further increase the demands placed on the individual. 23, 62 Continued exposure to adverse sensory conditions, in conjunction with the sustained effort of sensory masking or persistent override of natural sensory responses, can leave Autistic people increasingly vulnerable to distress and exhaustion.

text.text: In our current work, one participant described their process with loud environmental noise, "the sound is just so overwhelming all of me is focusing on just getting through that, leaving no energy left."
Another aspect worth exploring is the role of hypervigilance in masking from a sensory perspective.
Hypervigilance is a multifaceted process involving threat detection, sensory processing, cognitive appraisal, and physiological responses.
Understanding how these interacting processes influence sensory experiences may help explain why sustained sensory masking can be cognitively and physically demanding.

Hypervigilance involves neuroception, or the constant detection of threat via subconscious processes. 63 From a sensory perspective, it involves a state of heightened sensory alertness, often associated with a fight-or-flight response, in anticipation of potential threats or dangers-particularly in hostile or inhospitable sensory environments. 64 Additional processing of neuroceptive information involves the integration of interoceptive signals from within the body and external sensory signals, alongside affective (emotional) and cognitive processes in response to the physical and social worlds. 63 This may include acute awareness of fluorescent lighting, background noise, or nearby movement.

text.text: As such, hypervigilance engages with both subconscious and conscious cognitive functions.

The complex interplay between hypervigilance and the suppression of instinctive sensory responses adds further cognitive strain, 11, 65 intensifying the demands Autistic people face when navigating sensory environments. 26, 27 For example, an Autistic person in unpredictable and sensorily busy environments, such as a busy shopping mall or classroom, may be hyperaware of every sound, vibration, and movement in the space, while simultaneously suppressing their instinct to cover their ears or stim in response to the overwhelm, to avoid drawing attention or being judged.

text.text: Autistic people's responses to such environments may include autonomic responses, or involuntary physiological responses to perceived threat, which can involve dysregulation and difficulty returning to baseline.

This autonomic activity may be reflected in measures such as heart rate variability (HRV), the variation in time between successive heartbeats, with lower HRV associated with greater anxiety and reduced autonomic flexibility. 66, 67 Although these relationships have not yet been directly examined in sensory masking, physiological indicators of autonomic regulation may provide one potential avenue for investigating the mechanisms and longer-term consequences of sustained hypervigilance.

text.text: Over time, sustained sensory masking may have cumulative effects.

Continually suppressing, overriding, or dismissing sensory responses may contribute to disruptions in interoceptive processing, including difficulty identifying or responding to internal states such as fatigue, distress, or sensory discomfort. 68, 69 Reduced access to or trust in internal bodily signals may further contribute to exhaustion, dysregulation, distress, and difficulty recognizing needs for rest, recovery, or sensory regulation. 35 Autistic burnout can further reduce one's ability to prioritize and ignore sensory inputs, adapt to complex sensory environments, or tolerate hostile sensory stimuli. 19, 22 These cumulative effects may negatively impact well-being, contributing to depression, anxiety, trauma-related experiences, Autistic burnout, and even suicidal thoughts. 11, [19] [20] [21] These effects can, in turn, limit everyday participation and overall quality of life. 23, 70 This reduction of access to and trust in interoceptive input may also lead to depersonalization, in further detachment from one's own body, mind, or identity.

text.text: In the long term, without opportunities for self-regulation or reprieve, the cumulative effects of sustained masking, sensory overload, burnout and hypervigilance may contribute to trauma-related responses, sometimes resembling dissociation. 21, 71 Trauma can include big "T" trauma such as bullying or violence due to sensory expressions, or small "t" trauma, for example, feeling overwhelmed daily at school. 3, 20, 72 Autistic people may feel detached from their bodies or emotions or experience the world as distant or unreal-experiences that may arise in the context of prolonged sensory masking. 33, 68 When dissociation occurs, sensory experiences may become numbed, distorted, or intensified, reflecting a disconnection from one's environment. 71 While dissociation can serve as a short-term coping strategy, 73 its long-term effects are often detrimental, contributing to mental health issues, difficulties with concentration and memory, and physical symptoms such as numbness and reduced pain awareness. 74 Recovery from Unwanted or Sustained Sensory Masking.

text.text: Given the cumulative toll of sustained masking or persistent override of a sensory response, it is essential to explore approaches that may be helpful in supporting Autistic people to engage with sensory environments while minimizing the need to suppress their actual responses.

Considering sensory masking as another dimension of masking may extend our understanding of Autistic sensory experiences beyond traditional behavioral descriptors of hyper-and hyporesponsivity by recognizing that sensory responses may also be shaped by masking processes.

This does not imply that all sensory responses involve autonomous choice; rather, sensory responses may reflect multiple interacting processes, including sensory responsivity, context, lived experience, selfregulation, and, in some instances, sensory masking as an autonomous choice. 4, 10, 20, 33, 54 Autistic people often engage in self-regulatory behaviors to manage sensory overwhelm. 75, 76 One way this can occur is through the use of individualized, self-selected sensory input or strategies to support regulation and predictability within the environment. 76, 77 Examples include stimming, fidgeting with objects, seeking specific textures, or listening to familiar sounds or music.

text.text: In our current empirical work, one Autistic participant described their experience with background noise as increasing their ability to focus, "This is just normal background noise, it's kind of reassuring to have this kind of noise going on, as it helps me know where I am in space and what's going on around me."
These strategies can serve as an "inthe-moment" tool 3 to support self-regulation and help restore a sense of stability or return to "baseline" in a versatile or overwhelming sensory environment.

These strategies are consistent with concepts developed by the Autistic community such as sensory toolkits or "sensory diets." 75, 78 Importantly, the use of sensory toolkits or other sensory regulation strategies should not necessarily be interpreted as sensory masking.
text.formatted: These strategies are consistent with concepts developed by the Autistic community such as sensory toolkits or "sensory diets." <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">75,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">78</ref> Importantly, the use of sensory toolkits or other sensory regulation strategies should not necessarily be interpreted as sensory masking.

text.text: The same sensory behavior may function as regulation or masking depending on its context and purpose; sensory masking may occur when a preferred or instinctive sensory response is suppressed, inhibited, or modified in response to environmental or social expectations or anticipated repercussions.

Despite their functional and regulatory value, these selfregulatory behaviors-particularly stimming-are deeply misunderstood and pathologized. 41, 79 Many therapeutic approaches continue to focus on reducing or eliminating these behaviors. 80, 81 As a result, Autistic people often report feeling unsafe or discouraged from utilizing sensory selfregulatory strategies in public places like schools, workplaces and community settings. 41, 54 Furthermore, an existing body of Autistic-led research has emphasized that sensory self-regulation is not merely a coping strategy but a core aspect of Autistic identity and well-being. 3, 41 Restricting access to these self-regulatory strategies can leave Autistic people dysregulated and distressed, ultimately limiting their ability to participate fully in everyday life. 54 Supporting sensory unmasking.

text.text: More broadly, unmasking refers to the process of reducing or no longer consciously or unconsciously suppressing Autistic responses when it feels safe to do so.

From a sensory perspective, this may involve developing awareness of and responding to sensory experiences and needs that may previously have been suppressed or overridden, and, where appropriate, allowing sensory preferences and responses to be experienced or expressed.
Sensory masking in autism is a complex adaptation to navigate a world that often does not cater to Autistic sensibilities.
It is deeply intertwined with feelings of fear of negative evaluation 7, 8 and the deep need for safety.
text.formatted: It is deeply intertwined with feelings of fear of negative evaluation <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8</ref> and the deep need for safety.

text.text: Unmasking may require courage and vulnerability-facilitated by trust-to navigate the uncertainty and risks associated with expressing oneself in ways that may differ significantly from neuronormative expectations. 2, 10, 31, 82 Supporting sensory unmasking may involve reconnecting with interoceptive signals, enabling and empowering individuals to identify and respond to internal cues in ways that support regulation and well-being. 33, 68, 83 Since sensory masking may be adaptive in some contexts, the goal is not to discourage all sensory masking.

text.text: Rather, efforts should focus on reducing the need for chronic or involuntary sensory masking by expanding Autistic people's autonomy, access to accommodations, and opportunities to regulate sensory experiences in ways that are flexible, supported, and self-determined.
Autistic people are, however, disproportionately at risk of vulnerability experiences and victimization, 84, 85 which may further complicate decisions around reducing masking as a strategy.
text.formatted: Autistic people are, however, disproportionately at risk of vulnerability experiences and victimization, <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">84,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">85</ref> which may further complicate decisions around reducing masking as a strategy.

text.text: These experiences can make the prospect of unmasking daunting for three reasons.

First, the fear of negative evaluation and rejection is heightened, potentially exacerbated by legitimate fears for physical and emotional safety in Autistic people who might already have experienced negative interactions when their authentic behaviors were visible. 7, 8, 10, 86 Second, unmasking would require Autistic people to understand their own sensory masking tendencies-particularly those subconscious, conditioned responses-which can be mentally and emotionally demanding to gain insights into. 62, 87 Third, societal stigma and misconceptions about autism can lead to misinterpretation of natural sensory responses or selfregulatory behaviors, further discouraging Autistic people from "dropping their guard." 5, 11, 82 These factors create a complex web of challenges that Autistic people must navigate when considering whether to unmask.

text.text: Central to supporting reductions in sensory masking (should an individual wish to) and the authentic expression of sensory responses or regulatory strategies is establishing a sense of safety through building trust, whether in people, environments, or within policies and systems. 88, 89 A sense of safety is pivotal for Autistic people to feel less fearful of or worried about negative evaluation, allowing them to unmask and/or engage in sensory self-regulatory behaviors. [90] [91] [92] Sensorially safe environments are those that are sensory-friendly, nonjudgmental, and inclusive, offering a sense of belonging, welcome and understanding. 26 Practically, this could mean allowing Autistic people to familiarize themselves with their sensory environments as familiarity could alleviate some of the required cognitive load that sensory masking would usually require. 43, 44 Other people, particularly those who are non-autistic, play a crucial role in facilitating safe expression of sensory needs, responses and self-regulatory strategies.

text.text: Trustworthiness can be demonstrated by accepting, empathizing and respecting Autistic person's unique sensory experiences and needs.

People can support Autistic people by creating environments that are sensory-friendly, such as reducing background noise, offering quiet spaces or being mindful of lighting and odors. [93] [94] [95] Encouraging and respecting the use of sensory self-regulatory techniques and personalized sensory "tools," whether it be sound or lighting choices, self-regulatory sensory expressions or tools like fidgets or weighted items, also demonstrates support.

text.text: Furthermore, fostering an atmosphere of acceptance and understanding-where Autistic people feel safe to express their sensory needs without fear of judgment and stigma is essential. 96 This support not only benefits Autistic people but also promotes a more inclusive and empathetic society, where diversity in sensory processing is recognized and accommodated.

text.text: In essence, supporting sensory unmasking is about creating spaces where everyone can thrive in their own unique way.

Having time and space for sensory reset can bring positive outcomes for Autistic people. 38, 77 When Autistic people feel safe to unmask, take time to regulate, and embrace and explore sensory joys, they may experience reductions in stress and anxiety that often come with sensory overload and suppression of natural sensory responses, and shift into a balance where sensory masking can be used as a tool when needed, but is not a persistent way of being. 20, 90 In addition, allowing for time to unmask in sensorially safe environments could allow Autistic people to recharge and reset, to participate more fully in social and professional settings as desired, improve the ability to engage, and overall, potentially enhancing a person's wellbeing and quality of life. 97 Engaging in monotropic states could also facilitate sensory reset.

text.text: Monotropism refers to a cognitive style characterized by intense focus on or deep immersion in specific interests or stimuli, which has been identified as a trait that is core to the Autistic experience in Autistic-led literature. 64, 98, 99 In sensory terms, the intense focus or deep immersion can often increase the ability to block out and ignore other sensory environmental stimuli. 64, 100 When Autistic people are able to engage deeply in their passions, the need for constant sensory masking may be reduced, as monotropic focus tends to filter out competing sensory input, 28, 32 thus facilitating sensory reset.

text.text: Ultimately, when masking of sensory responses is shaped by experiences of threat or chronic stress, it may become an automatic and undesirable response to overwhelming or unsafe environments. 71 In these cases, it can create a dissonance between a person and their sensory experiences, leading to long-term dysregulation, exhaustion, and difficulty recognizing or responding to sensory needs.

text.text: Nevertheless, if we can create safe spaces, normalize sensory self-regulation and expression, support sensory unmasking, and facilitate sensory reset, sensory masking can shift from being an involuntary survival mechanism to a tool that can be utilized with autonomy.

By combining these approaches, Autistic people can have more agency over when and how they engage with the world in a sensory-safe and enjoyable way, rather than being trapped in a constant state of hypervigilance, survival and suppression.

A sense of safety and trust, both in people and in the predictability of sensory environments, plays a crucial role in making this possible, ensuring that masking is not an imposed necessity but one tool among many for navigating the world.

First, while the extant literature has primarily focused on social masking, expanding research into the role of sensory masking could help gain a deeper understanding of its neurobiological mechanisms and impacts, including the developmental trajectory of these phenomena. 56, 91, 101, 102 Longitudinal studies could help track how sensory masking or the conscious or unconscious ongoing inhibition of sensory responses changes over time and contexts, its connection to certain strategies like sensory self-regulation and sensory expression, and its cumulative effects-such as burnout, hypervigilance, and dissociation.

text.text: It would also be useful to explore whether some environments make sensory masking more necessary, while others help reduce its impact.

Future research should also examine the relationship between sensory masking and broader processes such as impression management, including whether and how socially motivated suppression of sensory responses may differ between Autistic and non-autistic people in its underlying sensory experience, function, and consequences.

Second, developing approaches to better capture or measure sensory aspects of masking, similar to existing masking and camouflaging frameworks such as the Camouflaging Autistic Traits Questionnaire, 42, 103 could provide a structured and rigorous way to assess its prevalence and impact.

text.text: Future work should also consider how different methodological approaches may provide complementary insights into sensory masking: Qualitative interviews may explore lived experiences and how sensory masking develops and is understood; self-report measures may capture its frequency and perceived impacts; ecological momentary assessment may examine when and in which contexts sensory masking occurs in daily life; observational methods may capture behavioral expressions of sensory masking; and psychophysiological measures may help investigate associated physiological processes.

Future research is also needed to distinguish sensory masking from related sensory processes, including interoceptive differences, sensory hyporesponsivity, and sensory regulation, and to better understand how these processes overlap, diverge, and interact over time.

A greater understanding of sensory masking will not only contribute to autism research but also inform policy changes for workplaces, schools, and public spaces, supporting the development of environments that are more accessible and affirming for Autistic people. 70 Third, further research is needed to better understand the developmental trajectory of sensory masking across the lifespan, including how sensory suppression, self-regulation, and sensory expression may change over time and contexts. 35 Longitudinal research could examine how sensory masking develops and changes across life stages and contexts, including transitions from playgrounds and classrooms to workplaces, where sensory and social demands and the feasibility of sensory (un)masking may shift.

text.text: Retrospective qualitative approaches may also provide insight into how sensory masking begins, persists, and changes across the lifespan. 104 Research could explore how sensory masking emerges developmentally through repeated exposure to sensory overwhelm, social expectations, environmental demands, or the invalidation of sensory experiences.

text.text: It may also be important to investigate how prolonged sensory masking influences longterm outcomes such as burnout, hypervigilance, dissociation, interoceptive processing, and difficulties recognizing or responding to internal sensory and emotional states.
Finally, a key research question is how to support Autistic people in navigating sensory masking in ways that are safe, flexible and self-determined across contexts.
Research could explore whether sensory-friendly environments, personalized regulation tools, and broader community accommodations reduce the need for persistent or unwanted masking.

Research should also consider the intersection between sensory masking and other identity-based experiences, such as gender and cultural background, to understand how different factors influence sensory masking, sensory self-regulation and sensory self-expression. 105, 106 Research should also include investigating the sensory dimensions of masking with regard to stigma, and how stigma can be addressed and mitigated.

text.text: Masking may involve the suppression of responses, including sensory, as Autistic people navigate environments that can feel overwhelming, unsafe, or socially demanding.
It reflects the tension between authentic sensory experiences and societal expectations of "normal" sensory reactions, shaped by past experiences of sensory overload or experiential rejection.
Rather than representing a distinct or separate construct, the sensory dimensions of masking highlight how sensory experiences are embedded within broader masking processes.
While sensory masking as a strategy can help Autistic people function in unsupportive contexts, it also carries significant emotional and cognitive costs.

To reduce the need for masking, greater awareness and meaningful changes to sensory environments are essentialnot only to accommodate sensory processing differences, but to support Autistic people's autonomy to engage in sensory self-regulation or unmasking, ultimately creating sensory safety and time and space for reset.

Recognizing these sensory dimensions of masking as both adaptive and potentially burdensome invites more inclusive design, enabling Autistic people to participate more fully and authentically in everyday life.
